..
Issued at 314 PM EDT Sat Oct 3 2026

Early afternoon GOES-East Day Cloud Phase RGB imagery shows a 
shallow midlevel cloud deck overspreading the UP with some 
glaciation over far western Lake Superior and northern Wisconsin 
that suggests that scattered precipitation is likely. This is 
supported by increased reflectivity returns from KDLH radar, though 
the shallow nature of these showers is evident by reflectivity 
returns from the KMQT radar being minimal to none. RAP analysis 
shows a tightening pressure gradient over the western end of Lake 
Superior as a 1010mb Clipper Low over the ND/MN/MB tri-point 
contrasts against 1028mb high pressure centered east of Georgian 
Bay. Disturbed weather ahead of the Clipper's cold front will arrive 
throughout the rest of today and overnight tonight. The mean HREF 
arrival of precipitation over the western UP is around 21Z, though a 
couple hours earlier is also reasonable as stray cells ahead of the 
front are showing up on radar. Rain arrives in the central UP around 
00Z and in the east by 04Z tonight. By the time synoptic precip ends 
UP-wide around 12Z, mean HREF QPF totals are between a third and a 
half inch for the north half and around a quarter inch for the south 
half, which is a slightly wetter trend than previous runs. The 
precip will initially have to battle some surface dry air as current 
dewpoint depressions are as much as 20-25 degrees in some locations, 
but NAEFS vapor transport charts shows unseasonably high rates of 
moisture arriving in the region (top 10% of climatology), so by the 
time the main area of precipitation arrives tonight, the moisture 
present will be sufficient for that rainfall to occur.

Another aspect of the Clipper will be gusty winds. Both the strong 
gradient as well as significant pressure rises and falls will 
encourage strong wind gusts, first out of the south tonight and then 
out of the northwest in the Clipper's wake. In both wind direction 
regimes, the REFS shows chances of 30+ mph gusts near Lake Superior 
to be around 50% with 40-70% chances of 35 kt gales over the open 
waters of the lake. 

Along with gusty winds, the brisk northwest flow will bring cool air 
aloft, with the NAM showing 850mb temperatures over eastern Lake 
Superior of around -3C over a lake that is between 10-14 C at the 
surface. The NAM resolves this with 50-150 J/kg of CAPE, enough to 
support some lake enhanced and lake effect precipitation in the east 
overnight Sunday into Monday morning, though the NBM shows 
precip ending later Monday morning as mid-upper 1020s mb high 
pressure expands across much of the central CONUS and the 
resulting subsidence puts an end to precip over the UP.

The 500mb pattern stagnates somewhat into next week as there is 
little in the way to perturb the persistent ridging over western 
North America and persistent troughing over eastern North America. 
This leaves the UP in continental northwesterly flow, keeping the 
forecast mostly dry, and while surface high pressure will allow for 
some radiational warming to above normal temperatures for Tuesday 
(NBM highs in the low 70s for the west), radiational cooling will 
also allow for temperatures to regularly fall into the 30s and sub-
freezing overnight. The most impactful part of the forecast next 
week looks to be Tuesday, where a shortwave passing through northern 
Ontario will cause a Clipper Low to pass, though it will be too 
starved of moisture to cause precipitation. However, the mean wind 
gusts from the Euro ahead of the Clipper's cold front are above 30 
mph, so the combination of warm, dry weather and gusty winds could 
cause fire weather concerns, especially as dry, fallen leaves 
increase the volatility of the ground fuels, although the current 
forecast is for RHs to remain above 40%, so the fire weather is not 
an immediate cause for alarm, but a forecast worth monitoring.
